text: Marcus sat on the back step with his coffee going cold and watched the light slide along the fence. He had been a structural engineer for twenty-two years, and for most of them his mornings began with a phone already buzzing against the counter. This morning the phone lay face down in the kitchen, and he had not gone to check it. The refinancing had closed. His daughter had called from university to say she had picked her major and did not intend to apologize for it. His knee, six weeks into physio, bent without the usual warning. Nothing was solved. The bridge contract was still three months behind, and his brother had not returned the call about their mother's house. Yet Marcus felt calm in a way he did not have to argue himself into. He finished the coffee anyway. A neighbor's dog barked twice and stopped. Somewhere a leaf blower started and quit. He stayed where he was, hands loose around the mug, and let the morning be exactly the size it was. The calm did not feel like a reward. It felt like the ordinary weight of a body that had finally stopped bracing for a blow that was not coming.

Throwaway account because my wife reads my main one. Ten months after my dad's stroke I think I'm finally calm about it, and I don't trust it. For most of last year I ran on adrenaline: rehab schedules in a spreadsheet, endless calls with the insurance people, a standing argument with my sister about the nursing home. Now the spreadsheet is mostly closed. Dad walks with a frame to the mailbox and complains about the soup, which is the most him thing he does. I went to a physio appointment on Tuesday and realized I had not checked my email in the car. I just drove and listened to a podcast about bridges. Calm is a strange feeling after a year of being wired. A friend said it might be grief arriving late, and I am not sure I want to unpack that on a forum. I am writing because I want to know whether other caregivers had this flat, almost detached calm once things settled. I felt like I should be more upset. Instead I felt calm and a bit distant, like a waiter after a long dinner service. Did it come back to normal for you? How long before you stopped waiting for the next phone call?

Dear Priya, I owe you a proper reply to your message from March, when you asked how I was really doing. Honest answer: better than I have been in years, and it still surprises me. The divorce papers were signed in June. The house sale closed in August. Ben has every second weekend and seems to like the new arrangement more than I expected, which I credit mostly to his therapist and partly to his new dog. I took the job in Leeds after all, the one I kept finding reasons not to apply for. The first month I kept waiting for the familiar tightening in my chest on Sunday evenings. It did not come. Now I walk to the market on Saturdays and buy far too much cheese. The calm is new, and I keep checking it, the way you check a healing cut. I feel calm in a way I have not felt since before my father died. I think I had mistaken being busy for being fine. You always said I did that, and you were right, and I hate it. Come up in October if you can. I will cook the rice you like, badly, and we can sit by the window and not talk about anything urgent. Love, Hannah.

Tuesday. Woke at six without the alarm and lay still for a while listening to the radiator tick. Made oatmeal with the cinnamon Mum sent, the one that smells like her kitchen. Walked the long way to the bus, past the closed bakery and the bench with the brass plaque nobody reads. Fog on the canal, a heron standing in it like it had all day. At work I finished the report on the ferry timetable and did not reopen it three times. Lunch on the wall outside with a sandwich I actually tasted. Phone stayed in my bag until four. Called Dan about the garden fence; he laughed at my drawing of the gate. Got home before dark, which hasn't happened since August. Peeled potatoes slowly. Lit the stove and sat with a book I have been meaning to finish since spring, reading the same page twice on purpose. Tomorrow the appointment with the surgeon is at nine. I have a list of questions and I have decided I can ask them in a plain voice. Bed at ten. Window open a crack. The street is empty except for a cat crossing under the lamp, unhurried, like it owns the hour.

The ferry pulled out at seven and Ines stood at the stern with a paper cup going warm in her hands. Behind her the town shrank to a row of white fronts and a church tower with its clock slightly wrong. She had not planned to come back here at fifty-four, and she had planned not to cry about it, and so far she had managed neither. Her sister's hospital bed was in the front room now, and the nurse had shown her how to change the dressing without making Rosa wince. The will was in a drawer. The keys to the apartment in the city sat on a hook she would have to remember to return. On deck a man was feeding gulls from a bag of bread rolls, and a girl in a yellow raincoat counted the wake aloud. Ines watched the water fold back on itself in long, unhurried lines. Her hands were steady on the rail. She noticed this the way she might notice a stranger's face in a window. The island had always been loud in her memory, all wind and arguments. Today the sea simply moved, and she moved with it, and when the coffee was finished she set the cup on the bench and sat down beside it, in no hurry to be anywhere at all.
